title: When should you CHOOSE a UUID key vs AVOID it — use it when you need decentralized/coordination-free unique IDs (distributed systems, DB sharding, merging/offline-sync data, or non-guessable public identifiers); avoid it (prefer auto-increment / sequences, or at least a time-ordered UUIDv7) for heavy-write relational tables (random-UUID index fragmentation), tight storage/bandwidth (16 bytes vs 4–8), when you need chronologically sortable IDs, and simple single-node apps?
shortTitle: When should you CHOOSE a UUID key vs AVOID it

s1_definition.profdef: Choose a UUID key when you need identifiers minted independently by many actors without a central coordinator — distributed systems, sharded databases, offline-first clients that sync later, or public identifiers that must not be guessable or enumerable. Avoid a random UUID when the table is write-heavy and relational, when storage and bandwidth are tight, when you need chronologically sortable keys, or when the app is a simple single node — in those cases prefer auto-increment or a database sequence, or at minimum a time-ordered UUIDv7 that keeps uniqueness and ordering without coordination.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a UUID is like letting every branch, ATM, and mobile app mint its own globally-unique reference number on the spot without phoning head office for the next number. That is essential when branches are offline or when you later merge their records, and it is great for public reference numbers that customers should not be able to guess or count. But for the central high-speed transaction ledger that runs on one cluster and must stay compact and time-ordered, a simple running counter from the central sequence is tidier, smaller, and faster. You pick the tool by whether coordination-free generation is actually needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use a UUID when many actors must mint ids with no coordination or when ids must be unguessable; avoid random UUIDs for compact, write-heavy, sortable single-node tables — then prefer auto-increment or UUIDv7.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Choose a UUID key when you need identifiers minted independently by many actors without a central coordinator — distributed systems, sharded databases, offline-first clients that sync later, or public identifiers that must not be guessable or enumerable. Avoid a random UUID when the table is write-heavy and relational, when storage and bandwidth are tight, when you need chronologically sortable keys, or when the app is a simple single node — in those cases prefer auto-increment or a database sequence, or at minimum a time-ordered UUIDv7 that keeps uniqueness and ordering without coordination.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a UUID is like letting every branch, ATM, and mobile app mint its own globally-unique reference number on the spot without phoning head office for the next number. That is essential when branches are offline or when you later merge their records, and it is great for public reference numbers that customers should not be able to guess or count. But for the central high-speed transaction ledger that runs on one cluster and must stay compact and time-ordered, a simple running counter from the central sequence is tidier, smaller, and faster. You pick the tool by whether coordination-free generation is actually needed.

**One line to remember:** Use a UUID when many actors must mint ids with no coordination or when ids must be unguessable; avoid random UUIDs for compact, write-heavy, sortable single-node tables — then prefer auto-increment or UUIDv7.

sections.s2_technical:
You choose a UUID when generation must be decentralized. In a distributed system many services create records at once, and asking a central sequence for the next number becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure; a UUID lets each node mint a guaranteed-unique id locally. The same applies to database sharding, where each shard must create non-colliding ids without talking to the others, and to offline or mobile clients that create records while disconnected and sync them later without renumbering.

You also choose a UUID for public identifiers that should not be guessable or enumerable. If your URL exposes an auto-increment order id like 1001, an attacker can simply try 1002, 1003 and enumerate every order — an insecure-direct-object-reference risk. A random UUID in the URL cannot be guessed or counted, which protects against enumeration.

You avoid a random UUID for heavy-write relational tables because, as covered earlier, random keys fragment the primary-key B-tree and slow inserts. You avoid it under tight storage or bandwidth because a UUID is 16 bytes versus 4 or 8 for an integer, and in InnoDB it is embedded in every secondary index, multiplying the cost. You avoid it when you need chronologically sortable ids, because a random UUID carries no time information. And you avoid it for simple single-node apps, where a database sequence is simpler, smaller, and perfectly sufficient.

The balanced middle path is a time-ordered UUIDv7. It keeps the decentralized, coordination-free uniqueness of a UUID, but its leading timestamp restores insert locality and approximate sortability, so it is the right default when you genuinely need UUID properties but also care about write performance. A senior nuance: never expose an internal auto-increment key in a public API even if you use it internally — use a separate opaque public id — and remember a UUID is an identifier, not a security token, so it must not replace proper authorization.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The mobile app lets customers create payment requests while offline, syncing when connectivity returns. A central sequence cannot be reached offline. This is exactly when to choose a UUID so each device mints unique ids independently.

Problem 2 — Public payment-request URLs must not be guessable or countable by attackers. This is exactly the unguessable-public-identifier case for a UUID.

Problem 3 — The internal high-throughput ledger runs on a single cluster, must stay compact, and is queried by time. This is exactly where auto-increment or UUIDv7 beats a random UUID.

The mini-project builds a payment-request service: the public-facing request id is a UUID for offline minting and unguessability, while the internal ledger uses a compact sequence, demonstrating choosing the right key per table.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a mobile device, currently offline, creates a payment request and mints its own UUID for it.

Step 1 — Offline, the device generates a UUID for the request. It does not contact any central sequence, which it could not reach anyway; the UUID is guaranteed unique by its sheer randomness and version structure.

Step 2 — When the device reconnects, it sends the request with its device-minted UUID. The service stores it as the `request_id` primary key. Because the id came from the device, no renumbering or coordination is needed on sync.

Step 3 — The public URL for this request uses the UUID, so an attacker cannot guess or enumerate other requests by incrementing a number, which protects customer data.

Step 4 — The service then posts a ledger entry. The ledger is central, write-heavy, and queried by time, so its primary key is a compact 8-byte auto-increment sequence that stays dense in the B-tree and sorts chronologically.

Step 5 — The two tables deliberately use different key strategies: a UUID where decentralized, offline, unguessable generation matters, and a sequence where compactness, write throughput, and time ordering matter. Each table gets the key that fits its job.

```text
2026-10-25 15:53:13 INFO  PaymentRequestService - Accepted payment request 018f2a1c-... (UUID: offline-minted, unguessable)
2026-10-25 15:53:13 INFO  PaymentRequestService - Posted ledger entry 90241 (BIGINT sequence: compact, time-ordered)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The decision to use a UUID key comes down to whether you genuinely need decentralized, coordination-free identifier generation, or unguessable public identifiers. You choose a UUID when many actors must mint ids independently — distributed systems where a central sequence would be a bottleneck, sharded databases where each shard must avoid collisions without talking to the others, and offline or mobile clients that create records while disconnected and sync later without renumbering. You also choose a UUID for public identifiers that must not be guessable or enumerable, because an auto-increment id in a URL lets an attacker simply count upward and enumerate every record.

You avoid a random UUID when those properties are not needed and their costs hurt. Heavy-write relational tables suffer from random-UUID index fragmentation and slower inserts. Tight storage or bandwidth makes the 16-byte UUID expensive versus a 4 or 8 byte integer, especially in InnoDB where it is embedded in every secondary index. Workloads that need chronologically sortable ids cannot use a random UUID because it carries no time. And simple single-node apps are better served by a plain database sequence, which is smaller and simpler. When you do need UUID properties but still care about write performance, the balanced choice is a time-ordered UUIDv7, which keeps coordination-free uniqueness while restoring insert locality and approximate ordering.

At the National Bank of India I applied this per table rather than globally. Our mobile app creates payment requests offline and syncs later, and the public URLs for those requests must not be guessable, so the request id is a UUID minted on the device. But the internal ledger is central, write-heavy, and queried by time, so its primary key is a compact auto-increment sequence that stays dense and sorts chronologically. Each table got the key that matched its actual needs.

The nuance I always add is that I never expose an internal auto-increment key directly in a public API even when I use it internally — I pair it with a separate opaque public identifier — and I remind people that a UUID is an identifier, not a security token, so it never replaces proper authorization checks.
